questions.stem: A 27 year old man collapses at a bus stop. A witness says he first complained of a strange feeling rising from his stomach, then went stiff with his eyes open, cried out and had rhythmic jerking of all four limbs for 2 minutes. He bit the side of his tongue and was confused and drowsy for 30 minutes afterwards.
questions.q: Which seizure type is most likely?
questions.e: An aura, tonic stiffening then clonic jerking with open eyes, lateral tongue biting and post-ictal confusion is a generalised tonic-clonic seizure.

clues: went stiff with his eyes open
rhythmic jerking of all four limbs
steps.x: Tonic then clonic phase, eyes open, prolonged post-ictal confusion.

elim: Sudden loss of tone with no jerking.
Brief jerks without loss of consciousness.
Eyes are usually closed, and tongue biting with prolonged post-ictal confusion is unusual.
Recovery is rapid with a short post-ictal period.

steps.x: B: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Tonic, then clonic, then post-ictal confusion = GTCS.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has episodes several times a week in which both arms suddenly jerk, like an electric shock, making her spill her tea. Each lasts less than a second. She remains fully aware throughout and never falls or loses consciousness. Examination between episodes is normal.
questions.q: Which seizure type is most likely?
questions.e: Brief, shock-like, often bilateral jerks without loss of consciousness are myoclonic seizures.

clues: both arms suddenly jerk, like an electric shock
steps.x: Lightning-fast bilateral jerks with full awareness.

elim: Brief loss of awareness with staring, not shock-like jerks.
Loss of tone and falls, not jerks.
Awareness is lost with automatisms.
Loss of consciousness with prolonged jerking.

steps.x: E: Myoclonic seizure. Shock-like jerks, aware = myoclonic.

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy with developmental delay has episodes several times a day in which he suddenly drops to the floor, hitting his face. His teacher says his body goes completely floppy, there is no shaking and he gets up within a few seconds. He wears a protective helmet at school.
questions.q: Which seizure type is most likely?
questions.e: A sudden loss of muscle tone causing a 'drop attack' with no jerking is an atonic seizure.

steps.x: Sudden floppiness and falls without jerking.

elim: Staring without loss of tone or falls.
Stiffening and jerking with post-ictal confusion.
Shock-like jerks, not floppiness.
Needs a trigger with prodrome; not many times a day in a child.

steps.x: B: Atonic seizure. Drop attack with loss of tone = atonic.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has episodes in which she stops talking mid-sentence, stares, fiddles with her buttons and smacks her lips for about a minute. She does not respond to her husband during the episode and has no memory of it afterwards. She does not fall or jerk.
questions.q: Which seizure type is most likely?
questions.e: Altered awareness with automatisms and no recollection is a focal impaired-awareness (complex partial) seizure.

clues: fiddles with her buttons and smacks her lips
steps.x: Automatisms with lost awareness and amnesia.

elim: Lasts seconds in children, without prolonged automatisms and post-event amnesia of this kind.
Causes falls from loss of tone.
Awareness is preserved and the event is remembered.
Brief jerks with awareness.

steps.x: D: Focal impaired awareness seizure. Automatisms + no recollection = focal impaired awareness.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has episodes of tingling and twitching in his left hand lasting 1 minute. During each episode he can talk to his wife, knows exactly what is happening and remembers it clearly afterwards. He has no loss of consciousness. Examination between episodes is normal.
questions.q: Which seizure type is most likely?
questions.e: Focal motor or sensory symptoms with preserved awareness and recollection is a focal aware seizure.

clues: tingling and twitching in his left hand
steps.x: Focal symptoms with full awareness.

elim: Awareness is lost.
Awareness is lost and the event is not remembered.
Loss of consciousness with whole-body jerking.
Causes negative symptoms (weakness, numbness), not twitching.

steps.x: B: Focal aware seizure. Focal + aware throughout = focal aware seizure.

questions.stem: An 8 year old boy is referred because he 'daydreams' in class. During the clinic visit he is asked to breathe deeply and quickly; after a minute he stops, stares blankly with fluttering eyelids for 10 seconds, then carries on talking as if nothing happened. Neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on EEG?
questions.e: Brief absence seizures triggered by hyperventilation, with a normal examination between episodes, show 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave on EEG; EEG supports the clinical diagnosis.

clues: carries on talking as if nothing happened
steps.x: Hyperventilation-provoked brief staring spells in a child.

elim: Suggest temporal lobe (focal) epilepsy.
Suggests encephalopathy.
Seen in infantile spasms.
Typical of non-epileptic events, not absences.

steps.x: A: 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave discharges. Absence seizures: 3 Hz spike-and-wave.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has episodes that begin with an intense feeling that she has lived the moment before and a smell of burnt toast. Her partner then sees her chewing and smacking her lips for 1 minute. Afterwards she cannot find her words for 10 minutes. She had prolonged febrile seizures as a child.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of seizure onset?
questions.e: Déjà vu, olfactory hallucinations, oral automatisms and post-ictal dysphasia point to a temporal lobe focus, often from mesial temporal sclerosis.

steps.x: Déjà vu, olfactory aura, lip smacking and post-ictal dysphasia.

elim: Causes bizarre hyperkinetic posturing and Jacksonian march.
Causes visual phenomena such as flashing lights.
Causes sensory symptoms such as tingling.
Generalised seizures do not have this aura and automatisms.

steps.x: D: Temporal lobe. Psychic aura + oral automatisms + dysphasia = temporal lobe.

questions.stem: A 32 year old man has brief episodes, mostly at night, in which he suddenly thrashes and kicks his legs as if cycling, with his arms held in odd postures. Each lasts 30 seconds and he recovers almost immediately. On other occasions jerking starts in his right hand and spreads up to his shoulder.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of seizure onset?
questions.e: Bizarre posturing, hyperkinetic behaviour and a Jacksonian march (clonic jerking spreading proximally) indicate a frontal lobe focus.

clues: thrashes and kicks his legs as if cycling
steps.x: Hyperkinetic nocturnal events and a Jacksonian march.

elim: Not a cortical seizure source.
Causes visual symptoms.
Causes sensory disturbance, not hyperkinetic movement.
Causes déjà vu, smells and oral automatisms.

steps.x: B: Frontal lobe. Hyperkinetic + Jacksonian march = frontal lobe.

questions.stem: A 15 year old girl has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure under flashing strobe lights at a concert after staying up the night before. Her mother says that for a year she has had jerks of her arms within an hour of waking, and her teachers report frequent brief staring spells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is the triad of myoclonic jerks, absences and GTCS in adolescence, 1 to 2 hours after waking, triggered by sleep deprivation, alcohol or photic stimulation.

clues: jerks of her arms within an hour of waking
steps.x: Teenager with morning jerks, absences and a GTCS after sleep loss and strobes.

elim: Does not explain morning myoclonic jerks and GTCS in adolescence.
Hyperkinetic events, not morning jerks plus absences.
Does not cause myoclonus and photosensitivity.
Focal auras and automatisms.

steps.x: C: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Morning jerks + absences + GTCS in a teenager = JME.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman is brought in after a 12 minute episode of shaking at work, following a stressful meeting. Colleagues say her eyes were tightly shut, her head moved from side to side and her pelvis thrust forwards. Afterwards she cried. Her vital signs and capillary glucose are normal. Her brother has epilepsy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Non-epileptic attack disorder is linked to psychological stress, is more common in women and those with a family history of epilepsy, and features pelvic thrusting, side-to-side head movements, closed eyes, duration over 3 minutes and post-ictal weeping.

steps.x: Prolonged attack, eyes closed, pelvic thrusting, weeping after a stressor.

elim: Eyes are open in epileptic seizures and stereotyped pelvic thrusting with weeping is unusual.
Brief with automatisms, not 12 minutes of thrashing with closed eyes.
Eyes are open and attacks rarely last over 3 minutes.
Brief with rapid recovery, not prolonged shaking.

steps.x: D: Non-epileptic attack disorder. Closed eyes + pelvic thrusting + >3 min + weeping = NEAD.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man collapsed in a supermarket. A witness says he fell, his limbs jerked for 30 seconds and he was then drowsy, confused and did not know where he was for 40 minutes. He had wet himself. His ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which feature most strongly suggests an epileptic seizure rather than syncope?
questions.e: Vasovagal syncope has rapid recovery and a short post-ictal period; prolonged confusion afterwards favours an epileptic seizure.

clues: confused and did not know where he was for 40 minutes
steps.x: Long confusion after the event.

elim: Short jerks commonly occur in syncope too.
Not a distinguishing feature.
Does not distinguish the two.
Can occur in syncope and is a weak discriminator.

steps.x: D: Prolonged post-ictal confusion. Long post-ictal confusion = seizure; rapid recovery = syncope.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with focal epilepsy has been seizure-free for 3 years on lamotrigine. Four days ago her GP prescribed an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection. Today she has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. She has not missed doses, slept normally and has not drunk alcohol. Her sodium and glucose are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her breakthrough seizure?
questions.e: Quinolones such as ciprofloxacin lower the seizure threshold and can cause breakthrough seizures in epilepsy.

clues: an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection
steps.x: New antibiotic, then breakthrough seizure with no other trigger.

elim: Not a recognised trigger for seizures at normal doses.
Does not lower the seizure threshold.
Does not lower the seizure threshold.
Does not lower the seizure threshold.

steps.x: C: Ciprofloxacin. Quinolones (ciprofloxacin) lower the seizure threshold.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man had an unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure 5 months ago. He now has another, also at home, with no alcohol, drugs, sleep deprivation or head injury beforehand. Bloods including glucose and electrolytes are normal and he has fully recovered.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Epilepsy is a tendency to recurrent, unprovoked seizures caused by abnormal electrical activity, generally diagnosed after two or more unprovoked seizures.

clues: unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure 5 months ago
steps.x: Two unprovoked seizures.

elim: No features such as closed eyes or pelvic thrusting; tonic-clonic with no trigger.
No provoking factor such as alcohol, drugs or metabolic upset.
This is his second unprovoked seizure.
No trigger or prodrome, and a tonic-clonic seizure.

steps.x: A: Epilepsy. Two or more unprovoked seizures = epilepsy.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with epilepsy started having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home 8 minutes ago. Paramedics arrive and she is still convulsing, with no recovery of consciousness. Her oxygen saturation is 92% on 15 L oxygen and capillary glucose 5.6 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A seizure lasting over 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery, is convulsive status epilepticus; prehospital treatment is buccal midazolam or PR diazepam.

steps.x: Seizure over 5 minutes without recovery.

elim: No features such as closed eyes or pelvic thrusting; ongoing tonic-clonic seizure with hypoxia.
She is still actively convulsing.
Only after first and second-line drugs fail.
Recovery would be within seconds.

steps.x: A: Convulsive status epilepticus. Seizure >5 min = status epilepticus: treat now.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman has had two episodes of collapse with jerking. The witness accounts are unclear and she cannot remember either episode. Her examination, bloods, ECG and MRI brain are normal. The neurologist wants a test to support the clinical diagnosis of epilepsy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Epilepsy is a clinical diagnosis supported by EEG.

clues: two episodes of collapse with jerking
steps.x: Suspected epilepsy needing support for the diagnosis.

elim: Less sensitive than her normal MRI and does not show seizure activity.
For infection, not recurrent seizures.
Not a routine test to support the diagnosis.
Investigates syncope, not epilepsy.

steps.x: B: EEG. Epilepsy: clinical diagnosis supported by EEG.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with alcohol dependence is brought in fitting. He has been convulsing for 7 minutes. Paramedics have secured his airway and given high-flow oxygen; his oxygen saturation is 96%. IV access has been obtained.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: In status epilepticus check capillary blood glucose promptly to exclude hypoglycaemia (and correct hypoxia) while giving IV lorazepam.

steps.x: Ongoing seizure; exclude the reversible cause at once.

elim: Important later but not before excluding hypoglycaemia.
Not needed to start treatment of convulsive status.
Unsafe while fitting and not first.
Does not change immediate management.

steps.x: A: Capillary blood glucose. In status: check glucose straight away.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after a first generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home. She is now fully alert with a normal neurological examination. She takes no regular medications and does not drink alcohol. She has been vomiting and having diarrhoea for 3 days.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: After a first seizure, bloods including glucose and electrolytes look for a provoking cause such as hyponatraemia, especially with vomiting and diarrhoea.

clues: vomiting and having diarrhoea for 3 days
steps.x: A first seizure with a possible metabolic trigger.

elim: No suggestion of vascular pathology.
Done later via the first seizure clinic.
No features of CNS infection.
Arranged later to look for a structural cause.

steps.x: E: Serum glucose and electrolytes. First seizure: check glucose and electrolytes.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has had three focal seizures over 2 months, each starting with twitching of the left side of his face. He has no previous history of seizures. Examination is normal. Bloods are normal and an EEG shows right-sided focal abnormalities.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Once epilepsy is suspected, MRI brain looks for a structural cause, especially with new focal seizures in an adult.

steps.x: New-onset focal epilepsy in an adult.

elim: Not the test for a structural cause of focal seizures.
For parkinsonian syndromes.
No features of infection.
Already abnormal; imaging is needed to find the cause.

steps.x: D: MRI brain. Suspected epilepsy: MRI brain for a structural cause.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has drug-resistant focal seizures with an epigastric rising sensation, déjà vu and lip smacking. She had prolonged febrile convulsions at age 2. She is assessed for epilepsy surgery and has an MRI brain.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on MRI?
questions.e: Temporal lobe seizures often arise from mesial temporal (hippocampal) sclerosis, producing psychic and autonomic auras.

clues: epigastric rising sensation, déjà vu and lip smacking
steps.x: Temporal lobe epilepsy after childhood febrile convulsions.

elim: Not linked to this seizure type.
Would cause frontal lobe seizures.
Suggests multiple sclerosis.
Would cause visual seizures.

steps.x: C: Hippocampal sclerosis. Temporal lobe epilepsy: mesial temporal (hippocampal) sclerosis.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man had a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home last night. He is now fully recovered with a normal neurological examination. His glucose, electrolytes and ECG are normal. He drives to work.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Discharge with urgent referral to a first seizure clinic and advise him not to drive
questions.e: After a first seizure, refer to urgent outpatient neurology (first seizure clinic) and discharge; antiepileptic drugs are not started before specialist review except in exceptional circumstances. DVLA rules mean he must stop driving.

steps.x: First seizure, recovered, normal tests, a driver.

elim: Not needed as an inpatient.
He needs specialist review.
AEDs are only started before specialist review in exceptional circumstances.
Not started after a single seizure before specialist review.

steps.x: C: Discharge with urgent referral to a first seizure clinic and advise him not to drive. First seizure: discharge, urgent neurology review, no AED yet, no driving.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman is diagnosed with focal epilepsy after recurrent episodes of déjà vu followed by lip smacking and loss of awareness. Her MRI is normal. She uses condoms for contraception and may want children in a few years.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug?
questions.e: First-line treatment for focal seizures is lamotrigine or levetiracetam.

steps.x: Focal epilepsy in a woman of childbearing age.

elim: Sedating and not first-line.
Not first-line and discontinued in pregnancy.
Teratogenic; avoided in women of childbearing potential.
A second-line option for focal seizures.

steps.x: A: Lamotrigine. Focal seizures: lamotrigine or levetiracetam.

questions.stem: A 17 year old boy is diagnosed with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy after morning jerks and two generalised tonic-clonic seizures. His EEG shows generalised polyspike-and-wave. He has no other medical problems, takes no regular medicines and is about to start university. He wants treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug?
questions.e: Levetiracetam is preferred for myoclonic seizures; sodium valproate is avoided in both males and females of childbearing age.

steps.x: Myoclonic epilepsy in a young man.

elim: Can worsen myoclonic seizures.
For absence seizures only.
Can worsen myoclonic seizures and is not first-line.
To be avoided in both males and females of childbearing age.

steps.x: C: Levetiracetam. Myoclonic: levetiracetam; avoid valproate in anyone of childbearing age.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl has dozens of 10 second episodes a day of blank staring with eyelid flickering, after which she carries on as normal. Her EEG shows 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave. Her development and examination are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug?
questions.e: Absence seizures are treated first-line with ethosuximide.

steps.x: Typical absence epilepsy.

elim: Can worsen absence seizures.
Used for focal seizures, not absences.
Used for focal, GTCS, tonic and atonic seizures; not first-line here.
Can worsen absence seizures.

steps.x: B: Ethosuximide. Absence seizures: ethosuximide.

questions.stem: A 12 year old boy with a learning disability has frequent drop attacks in which he suddenly loses tone and falls without jerking, and other episodes where his whole body stiffens briefly. His EEG shows generalised abnormalities.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug?
questions.e: Tonic or atonic seizures are treated with lamotrigine.

steps.x: Atonic and tonic seizures.

elim: Can worsen tonic and atonic seizures.
For absence seizures.
For focal seizures.
Not first-line and has many side effects.

steps.x: D: Lamotrigine. Tonic or atonic seizures: lamotrigine.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has had three unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizures in a year. His MRI brain is normal and EEG shows generalised discharges. He works as a builder and has no other medical problems. He wishes to start treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug?
questions.e: Generalised tonic-clonic seizures are treated first-line with lamotrigine or levetiracetam.

steps.x: Generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy in an adult man.

elim: Second-line for focal seizures and may worsen generalised seizures.
Only for absence seizures.
Second-line for focal seizures only.
Not first-line due to side effects and interactions.

steps.x: D: Levetiracetam. GTCS: lamotrigine or levetiracetam.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with focal epilepsy has had ongoing seizures despite adequate doses of lamotrigine and then levetiracetam. Her neurologist starts carbamazepine. She currently takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and does not want to become pregnant.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate contraceptive advice?
o: Continue the combined pill at the usual dose
Switch to the levonorgestrel intrauterine system
questions.e: Carbamazepine is a second-line drug for focal seizures that interacts with hormonal contraception, so an IUS such as Mirena is preferred.

steps.x: An enzyme-inducing AED with hormonal contraception.

elim: Carbamazepine induces liver enzymes and makes it unreliable.
Also affected by enzyme induction.
Effectiveness is reduced by enzyme inducers.
Not a regular method.

steps.x: B: Switch to the levonorgestrel intrauterine system. Carbamazepine + contraception: use an IUS.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with generalised epilepsy is 30 weeks pregnant. She takes lamotrigine and folic acid 5 mg and has been seizure-free. She plans to breastfeed and asks whether she will need to stop her medication when the baby is born.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Add a second antiepileptic drug for labour
Stop lamotrigine after delivery to allow breastfeeding
questions.e: In pregnancy lamotrigine with 5 mg folic acid is used, oral AEDs continue through labour, breastfeeding is safe, and dual therapy is avoided.

steps.x: Pregnant woman with controlled epilepsy on lamotrigine.

elim: Dual therapy is more teratogenic and not needed.
Breastfeeding is safe on AEDs; stopping risks seizures.
Oral AEDs should continue in labour where tolerated.
Phenytoin has more side effects and offers no advantage.

steps.x: B: Continue lamotrigine; breastfeeding is safe. Epilepsy in pregnancy: lamotrigine + 5 mg folic acid, continue in labour, breastfeed.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman with focal epilepsy started a new antiepileptic drug 3 months ago. She has lost 6 kg without trying, has had an episode of right loin pain with haematuria, and says she struggles to find words at work.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Topiramate causes weight loss, renal stones and cognitive or behavioural change.

steps.x: Weight loss, renal stones and word-finding difficulty.

elim: Causes hyponatraemia and rash, not weight loss and stones.
Causes rash and rarely Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Causes gum hyperplasia and hirsutism.
Causes weight gain, not weight loss.

steps.x: E: Topiramate. Topiramate: weight loss, stones, cognitive slowing.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man started lamotrigine for generalised epilepsy 3 weeks ago. He now has fever, sore eyes, painful ulcers in his mouth and a spreading rash with blisters on his trunk. His temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 110 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Lamotrigine can cause a blistering rash and, rarely, Stevens-Johnson syndrome; it must be stopped immediately and the patient admitted.

steps.x: Mucosal ulcers and a blistering rash soon after lamotrigine.

elim: Risks progression of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Any dose may continue the reaction.
Not a herpes infection.
This is a drug reaction, not cellulitis.

steps.x: E: Stop lamotrigine and admit urgently. Lamotrigine rash: stop at once.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has taken an antiepileptic drug for many years. He has swollen, overgrown gums, coarse facial features and increased body hair. He also has numbness in both feet and a macrocytic anaemia with low folate.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Phenytoin causes gum hyperplasia, hirsutism, coarse facial features, peripheral neuropathy and megaloblastic anaemia from folate depletion.

steps.x: Gum hyperplasia, hirsutism, neuropathy and folate deficiency.

elim: Causes hyponatraemia and rash.
Causes rash.
Causes mood and behaviour change.
Causes weight gain, tremor and hair loss.

steps.x: D: Phenytoin. Phenytoin: gums, hair, coarse face, neuropathy, folate loss.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman with generalised epilepsy has been seizure-free for 3 years on levetiracetam. She has no other medical problems, her EEG is now normal and she does not drive. After discussing the risk of recurrence, she wishes to try coming off her medication.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Continue lifelong as withdrawal is never possible
Taper the dose slowly over 2 to 3 months
questions.e: AEDs can be considered for withdrawal after more than 2 years seizure-free, tapering over 2 to 3 months.

steps.x: Seizure-free over 2 years and wants to stop.

elim: Withdrawal can be considered after 2 years seizure-free.
Abrupt withdrawal can provoke seizures.
No reason to change drug.
The threshold is over 2 years.

steps.x: D: Taper the dose slowly over 2 to 3 months. Withdrawal after >2 years seizure-free, taper over 2 to 3 months.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy has frequent seizures despite trials of three appropriate antiepileptic drugs. He is not a candidate for epilepsy surgery. His parents ask whether any non-drug treatment might help alongside his medication.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional intervention?
questions.e: A ketogenic diet may be used as an adjunct in some patients with drug-resistant epilepsy.

clues: despite trials of three appropriate antiepileptic drugs
steps.x: Drug-resistant epilepsy in a child.

elim: Not a treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy.
No role unless coeliac disease is present.
The ketogenic diet is low carbohydrate.
Would worsen seizures.

steps.x: D: Ketogenic diet. Drug-resistant epilepsy: consider a ketogenic diet adjunct.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that started 10 minutes ago. He has not received any treatment. His airway is supported and he is on high-flow oxygen. His capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L. IV access is in place.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Rapid sequence induction with general anaesthesia
questions.e: First-line for convulsive status epilepticus with IV access is IV lorazepam 4 mg, repeated once if needed.

steps.x: Convulsive status with IV access and no treatment yet.

elim: Prehospital option when there is no IV access.
Second-line after two doses of benzodiazepine.
Second-line after two doses of benzodiazepine.
For refractory status after second-line drugs.

steps.x: C: IV lorazepam 4 mg. Status: IV lorazepam 4 mg, up to two doses.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman is still having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure 25 minutes after arrival in the Emergency Department. She has had two doses of IV lorazepam 4 mg. Her capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L and oxygen saturation is 95% on high-flow oxygen.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: A third dose of IV lorazepam
questions.e: If two benzodiazepine doses fail, second-line is IV levetiracetam, IV phenytoin (most preferred) or IV sodium valproate.

clues: two doses of IV lorazepam 4 mg
still having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure
steps.x: Status continuing after two benzodiazepine doses.

elim: The maximum is two doses.
For eclamptic seizures only.
Oral route is inappropriate during a seizure.
Another benzodiazepine; a second-line agent is needed.

steps.x: C: IV phenytoin. After two lorazepam doses: IV phenytoin, levetiracetam or valproate.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man with convulsive status epilepticus has received two doses of IV lorazepam and an infusion of IV levetiracetam. Forty-five minutes after onset he is still convulsing. His airway is maintained with adjuncts and oxygen saturation is 91%.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Await the effect of levetiracetam for 2 hours
questions.e: Refractory status epilepticus, continuing after second-line treatment, needs ITU admission and general anaesthesia.

steps.x: Status persisting despite first and second-line drugs.

elim: Ongoing seizures cause brain injury; escalate now.
Treatment must not be delayed.
Benzodiazepines are maximised and now less effective.
Wrong route and setting.

steps.x: D: ITU admission with general anaesthesia. Refractory status: ITU and general anaesthesia.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman who is 36 weeks pregnant has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure on the antenatal ward. She has no history of epilepsy. Her BP is 168/112 mmHg and urine dipstick shows 3+ protein.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Seizures in pre-eclampsia (eclampsia) are treated with IV magnesium sulphate, not standard antiepileptic drugs.

steps.x: Seizure with hypertension and proteinuria in pregnancy.

elim: Standard AEDs are not used for eclampsia.
Not the treatment for eclamptic seizures.
Inferior to magnesium in eclampsia.
Does not treat the seizure.

steps.x: C: IV magnesium sulphate. Eclampsia: IV magnesium sulphate.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man is on the neurosurgical ward 3 days after a severe traumatic brain injury in a motorbike crash. He has had two seizures today that have not settled with a single dose of IV lorazepam. His airway is secure.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antiepileptic drug?
questions.e: IV phenytoin is used if seizures are uncontrolled after first-line treatment, including in the first 7 days after traumatic brain injury.

clues: 3 days after a severe traumatic brain injury
not settled with a single dose of IV lorazepam
steps.x: Early post-traumatic seizures not controlled by a benzodiazepine.

elim: For eclampsia.
For absence seizures, and too slow here.
Too slow to titrate in the acute setting.
Another benzodiazepine rather than a longer-acting agent.

steps.x: A: IV phenytoin. Early post-TBI seizures: IV phenytoin.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman's convulsive seizure stops within a minute of IV lorazepam being given in the Emergency Department. She had been convulsing for 9 minutes with a capillary glucose of 5.4 mmol/L. A pharmacology student watching asks how the drug works at the neuronal level.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action?
questions.e: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A receptor-mediated chloride influx, hyperpolarising neurons.

steps.x: A benzodiazepine terminates the seizure.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man with focal epilepsy is well controlled on lamotrigine. He asks how the drug stops neurons from firing too much. His previous neurologist had used phenytoin, which he says works 'in the same way'.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action shared by both drugs?
o: Binding to synaptic vesicle protein SV2A
questions.e: Phenytoin and lamotrigine act on voltage-gated sodium channels, reducing repetitive high-frequency firing.

steps.x: Two drugs that share a target.

elim: Levetiracetam.
Benzodiazepines.
Vigabatrin and partly valproate.
Ethosuximide.

steps.x: B: Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels. Phenytoin and lamotrigine: sodium channel blockade.

questions.stem: A 16 year old girl with generalised epilepsy asks why her neurologist will not prescribe sodium valproate, which controls seizures well for her cousin. She is sexually active and does not want to use contraception long term.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: It acts only on absence seizures
It increases GABA and blocks sodium and calcium channels but is highly teratogenic
It is a benzodiazepine causing dependence
It only acts on focal seizures
questions.e: Sodium valproate increases GABA availability and blocks sodium and calcium channels, giving broad efficacy, but carries a high teratogenic risk.

steps.x: A girl of childbearing potential asking about valproate.

elim: Valproate has broad efficacy.
A side effect of phenytoin.
Valproate is not a benzodiazepine.
It is broad-spectrum.

steps.x: C: It increases GABA and blocks sodium and calcium channels but is highly teratogenic. Valproate: broad-spectrum but highly teratogenic.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man in convulsive status epilepticus is brought in after a long ambulance journey. He received no treatment until arrival, 50 minutes after the seizure began. IV lorazepam 4 mg is given twice with no effect. The registrar explains why the drug failed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Internalisation of GABA-A receptors during prolonged seizures
Lorazepam does not cross the blood-brain barrier
Upregulation of sodium channels by lorazepam
questions.e: As status epilepticus continues GABA-A receptors are internalised, so seizures become increasingly resistant to benzodiazepines; this is why early treatment is urgent.

steps.x: Benzodiazepines failing after a long seizure.

elim: Glucose does not block lorazepam binding.
It does, and works well early.
Lorazepam is not an enzyme inducer.
Not a mechanism of benzodiazepine failure.

steps.x: B: Internalisation of GABA-A receptors during prolonged seizures. Long seizures internalise GABA-A receptors: treat early.

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman has generalised tonic-clonic seizures with loss of consciousness from the very start, without any warning or aura. Her EEG shows bilateral, synchronous discharges at seizure onset. A student asks what is happening in the brain.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying mechanism?
o: Hypersynchronous discharges involving both hemispheres from onset
Single temporal lobe focus of hypersynchronous discharge
Transient loss of dopamine in the basal ganglia
questions.e: Seizures are abnormal, hypersynchronous electrical discharges from cortical neurons, either starting focally or involving both hemispheres from onset (generalised).

clues: bilateral, synchronous discharges at seizure onset
steps.x: Bilateral onset without aura.

elim: Multiple sclerosis or ADEM.
Syncope.
Would give an aura and focal onset.
Not a seizure mechanism.

steps.x: B: Hypersynchronous discharges involving both hemispheres from onset. Generalised seizures: both hemispheres from onset.
